extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, statesmen, and educated readers considering constitution design (late-18th-century American context)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the quality and practicability of constitutions and forms of government (republics, mixed governments, monarchies) with attention to separation of powers, checks and balances, representation, and historical experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of law as the rule and security of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws, which are the only possible rule, measure, and security of justice, can be the hire of protection for any course of time, in no other form of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that a government of laws (rather than of men) is essential: the laws must measure and secure justice over time. Examples and authority invoked include Cicero's notion that laws are the only possible rule, and the statement that a government of laws might justify calling a limited monarchy a republic if it truly operates under laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of property in the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The very name of a republic implies that the property of the people should be represented in the legislature, and decide the rule of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as part of Cicero's authority: property representation in the legislature is necessary for a republic. The text contrasts representation by property (houses) versus representation of persons, noting effects on equality and checks against licentiousness (discussion of arengo in St. Marino).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as necessary condition for a republic (not merely name)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the chief magistrate, senators, or people are unjust, the state is no longer a republic; unjust rulers or unjust collectives cannot be called a republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from classical authorities stress that 'when unjust is the king... or unjust the optimates... or unjust the people... there is no republic.' The page emphasizes substance (justice) over form or label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and division of powers (legislative, executive, judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should divide powers into separate branches (representatives/assembly, council/senate, and governor/executive) rather than collect all authority into one center.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes proposals to 'collect all authority into one center' (as Mr. Turgot suggested) and defends institutions that separate powers. Examples: English constitution's multiple bodies; American constitutions with distinct governor, senate, and assembly; St. Marino's capitaneos (executive), council (legislative), commissary (judicial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances / negative powers for branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Each division should have the power to defend itself (a negative) against the others; a proper equilibrium between branches is essential to preserve liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text praises the English balancing of powers and suggests giving each division a negative is what preserved democratic authority. The idea appears repeatedly as the core means to avoid tyranny and maintain stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical scale constraints favor representative government
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple, direct democracy (assembly of the whole people) is impracticable for large territories and populations; representation is necessary for effective governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks rhetorically how a half-million scattered people could assemble to govern directly and points out practical impossibilities (space, time). St. Marino (tiny population) contrasts with large American states to illustrate scale effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy) and equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful constitution often blends monarchical, aristocratical, and democratical elements and seeks an equilibrium among them rather than relying on one pure form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Marino, Sparta, Rome, and modern English and American examples are used to show mixed constitutions. The author contends that Americans have blended beneficial elements and that proper mixing avoids inconveniences of pure forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional safeguards against concentration (age, term limits, family restrictions, supermajorities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design features such as minimum ages, term limits, prohibitions on father and son serving together, restrictions on two members of the same family, and higher thresholds (e.g., two-thirds) for decisions help prevent concentration and abuse of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Marino's constitution provides examples: council members must be 25+, no son admitted during father's life, no two of same family, two-thirds confirmation for sentences. These are presented as checks limiting faction and family dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and impartial judiciary with structural protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial office should be insulated from local alliances and partisanship (e.g., by term lengths, external appointment, remuneration from public stock) to act as an effective check on other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Marino uses a foreigner as commissary (judge) chosen for three years and paid from public stock — an institutional design to avoid local feuds obstructing justice. The text highlights judiciary independence as a necessary check on executive and legislative powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms to ensure citizen participation and prevent factional capture
rubrics_metrics.description: Because low attendance in popular assemblies permits active factions to carry measures by intrigue, constitutions should include mechanisms to encourage or compel participation and to reduce the influence of small organized minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes St. Marino had to enact a law fining absence from the arengo because general disinclination to attend allowed active persons/parties to dominate. This example supports designing turnout-enforcement or mitigating institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical experience and long-term testing in institutional design
rubrics_metrics.description: Political institutions are experiments on human affairs and must be judged by long experience and stability; one should favor institutions with demonstrated longevity and adapted experience rather than speculative innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly appeals to the longevity of Teutonic institutions, Roman stability, and the long-lasting English balance; it cautions that political experiments cannot be done in a laboratory and require centuries to judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradualism: prefer gradual improvements and public education over abrupt constitutional overthrows
rubrics_metrics.description: If the people should aim for more, they should proceed by gentle, gradual means — improvements in general education and informing the public mind — rather than abrupt or violent change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author counsels against aiming for rapid revolutionary changes and recommends gradual advances through education to reform institutions safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual suitability: tailor institutions to size, wealth, and social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution must fit the particular circumstances of the people (population size, territory, poverty or wealth, social ties); small, intimate communities can sustain different arrangements than large, populous nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Marino's small, poor, close-knit society (where everyone knows everyone) can sustain forms that would fail in America. The author uses this to warn against copying institutions without considering local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid centralizing all authority in a single center
rubrics_metrics.description: Collecting all authority into one center (whether called 'the nation' or an assembly) risks practical confusion, factional domination, or despotism; distribution and delegation are needed for governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author critiques Mr. Turgot's proposal of collecting authority in 'one center' (the nation) as impracticable and logically circular; argues that such centralization would result either in despotism or in rule by a majority faction rather than true national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive function matters more than labels (form vs reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a government is called a 'republic' or 'limited monarchy' matters less than whether it functions as government of laws and preserves liberty; a limited monarchy governed by laws may rightly be termed a republic in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes a limited monarchy 'if it could in reality be what it pretends to be — a government of laws — might be justly denominated a republic.' Emphasizes practical operation over nominal classification.
